topic: software testing; variable-strength combinatorial testing; evaluation metrics; fault detection
status: bounded evaluation-design lead from one sampled 2018 full text and a targeted 2026 full-text preprint check; no independent reproduction
claim: The sampled FPSO paper demonstrates suite-size results, not fault-finding effectiveness: it compares best/mean generated sizes over 30 stochastic runs and excludes runtime, but never executes the suites against an SUT. A much newer CIT-metrics preprint reports correlations between static metrics and fault-detection effectiveness, including historical developer-confirmed faults, and names VCC as its best overall predictor; however, it does not evaluate FPSO and has unresolved internal inconsistencies (abstract: eight programs/32 scenarios; body: nine/36; front matter: 2018 JACM placeholders in a 2026 arXiv submission). Therefore the bounded opportunity is an FPSO/DPSO outcome replication with direct fault detection and a held-out metric-calibration test—not a claim that combinatorial metrics lack validation.
positive_evidence: The sampled FPSO study runs each configuration 30 times and reports best and mean test-suite sizes; runtime is explicitly excluded because implementations and environments differ.
DPSO achieves the strongest minimum-size results overall and usually the best means; FPSO obtains the best mean in some rows, so the original result is mixed rather than a universal win.

The 2026 arXiv v1 evaluates static combinatorial-suite metrics against fault-detection effectiveness; its PDF describes verified mutation faults for five SIR programs and real historical developer-confirmed faults for BusyBox, Drupal, and Linux Kernel.
The 2026 paper reports VCC as its best overall metric but explicitly notes strength-1 VCC can saturate prematurely and fail to reflect suite quality.
counterevidence: The FPSO result is not an actual-fault evaluation, but generated suite size is still a legitimate optimization objective when the required coverage is satisfied; absence of fault execution is an unmeasured endpoint, not evidence the method is ineffective.
The 2026 follow-up is direct positive evidence that some static CIT metrics can correlate with fault detection on its selected programs and faults, narrowing the earlier evidence gap.

The 2026 study is an arXiv v1; its abstract/body disagree on the number of programs and scenarios and its PDF front matter contains anomalous JACM 2018/placeholder DOI metadata. Those issues make its broad recommendation provisional pending artifact/data reconciliation.

A correlation of a metric with fault counts on selected historical/mutated faults does not establish causal improvement, deployment-defect yield, or that the metric transfers to FPSO-generated variable-strength suites.

sources.sections: Sections 6–8: 30-run design, size-only outcomes, Tables 3–5, 95% interval plots, runtime exclusion, stochastic caveat

falsifiable_test: On version-pinned variable-strength CIT models and executable SUTs, compare FPSO, DPSO, and established non-PSO generators across preregistered seeds. Match total generation-plus-execution compute, preserve each suite’s reported size and required coverage, execute against a deduplicated set of developer-confirmed historical faults plus non-equivalent mutants, and report per-seed fault yield. Separately test whether pre-execution VCC predicts held-out fault detection after controlling for suite size and strength. The lead weakens if FPSO’s size advantage consistently translates into equal-or-better direct fault yield at matched cost and VCC adds no predictive value beyond size/strength; it strengthens if results reverse across targets or the apparent metric relationship fails out of sample. This batch did not run the experiment.
limitations: One historical FPSO chapter and one unreconciled 2026 preprint; no generator replication, SUT execution, source-code/data artifact audit, or causal design. The new result should not be treated as a novelty claim or as proof that size-based optimization is invalid.

topic: software testing; continuous kernel fuzzing; fuzzing outcome measurement; bug lifecycle
status: bounded measurement-design lead from one sampled ISSREW 2019 full text and one targeted full-text RAID 2025 follow-up
claim: For the reviewed kernel-fuzzing studies, pending-report age and report-to-fix time are not interchangeable with a fuzzer’s time-to-discovery. The 2019 snapshot counts unresolved crash reports that may duplicate bugs and uses a single early observation date; SyzRetrospector later separates time while a bug is hidden/unfindable from time after it becomes findable but before the fuzzer discovers it. Its 559-case upstream Linux analysis reports mean D1=331.17 days and D2=73.94 days, but excludes hard-to-reproduce/build-failing cases and warns D2 is likely underestimated. This supports a distinct, falsifiable endpoint design, not a claim that these delays generalize to every kernel or fuzzer.
positive_evidence: The 2019 sampled paper reports more than 800 pending syzbot crash reports and different medians by kernel, while explicitly warning crash reports may not represent unique bugs and false positives/reproducibility are concerns.
The 2019 paper’s report-to-fix and commit-marker measures address downstream maintenance but do not operationalize when each bug first became fuzzable.
SyzRetrospector explicitly defines D1 as hidden/unfindable time and D2 as revealed-but-not-yet-discovered time; among 559 retrospectable Linux bugs, it reports means of 331.17 and 73.94 days.
In its random 50-bug manual check, SyzRetrospector judged 44 revealing factors correct (88%), providing a validation check beyond simply fitting timestamp distributions.
counterevidence: The 2019 study did analyze both pending age and time-to-fix, so it was not wholly blind to lifecycle time; it simply measured different stages than retrospective fuzzer reachability.
SyzRetrospector’s 88% revealing-factor check is encouraging, but it is a 50-case manual sample within one upstream-Linux cohort, not independent validation across operating systems.
SyzRetrospector began with 1,159 candidate bugs and excluded cases that failed reproduction/build requirements; the authors state this likely underestimates D2 for hard-to-find bugs.

The follow-up reconstructs upstream Linux history using custom patches and requires fixing commits and reproducers; its estimates cannot be assumed to apply to unresolved, unreported, BSD, or non-kernel bugs.

sources.sections: Sections II–IV; 2019 snapshot, distributions, method, and stated limitations
Sections III–V, VII–VIII, and X; definitions, 559-case analysis, manual validation, and bias discussion

falsifiable_test: Create a version-pinned Linux/BSD kernel bug cohort with deduplicated bug identities and explicit inclusion/censoring rules. For each confirmed bug, record introduction, first commit/configuration that made it reproducible by the relevant fuzzer, first fuzzer report, human confirmation, and patch/fix timestamps. Audit a blinded sample of retrospectively assigned revealing factors; report interval-censored D1, D2, report-triage, and fix distributions separately, then stratify by bug class, kernel, and reproducibility. The lead weakens if D1/D2 are negligible or do not change rankings versus report-to-fix under these cohorts; it strengthens if metrics differ materially or exclusions shift D2 estimates. No reconstruction was run in this batch.
limitations: Two studies with different units, time periods, populations, and endpoints; the later study is upstream Linux only and conditions on reproducibility/fix metadata. No unified cohort or new data analysis was performed; no cross-kernel causal claim.
